during the end credits jack black points at david bowie, lou reed, and the velvet underground in the middle of his after-school club's jam sesh and screams into the mic 'i do not know that guy!' . it's school of rock in miniature: easywatching because there's nothing new here; it is just a list of credits but for the whole film. the magical first instance when dewey discovers his students can play musical instruments sees the camera draw back from him specifically to frame all the children as a band as they play "smoke on the water"—the start of the school of rock as a group of equal members remains centred on him throughout, and on an intergenerational repurposing of the old culture. it's a narcissistic framing that is narratively contested by his insistence that all the kids have a say over their final song, but he is the one who persuades them, and when they come out again for their encore, the choice is made to focus on him before the camera turns up to the ceiling. that kind of authority is an abuse of power over children. joan cusack even repurposes 70s paedophile wooderson's 'all right, all right, all right!' catchphrase from dazed and confused to congratulate every last one of them. rocking out becomes intertextually associated with perverted forms of desire and age-as-authority. kids aren't the future, they're the past, and nobody knows who they are or what they're playing.

School of Rock is proof that if you shout loudly enough, people will call it a “classic.” Dewey Finn spends the whole film committing about 47 crimes before breakfast. He steals his roommate’s job, lies to an entire school, tricks the parents, ignores the curriculum, and somehow gets rewarded instead of getting escorted out by the police. Disney morals? Nope. Just pure chaos. Jack Black acts like he’s being paid by the decibel. Every five minutes he’s either screaming “ROCK!”, jumping on a desk, or pulling a face that looks like he just stubbed his toe. I was exhausted just watching him. The students are the only professionals in the building. They’re ridiculously talented, and somehow end up teaching themselves while Dewey’s masterclass consists of “play louder.” The story has more plot holes than Swiss cheese. Nobody checks his qualifications. Nobody questions why the “teacher” keeps disappearing with the class. Nobody thinks it’s weird that lessons have turned into rehearsals for a rock competition. Apparently common sense took the day off too. The Battle of the Bands is actually good—but that’s like saying the breadsticks were the best part of a terrible restaurant. Final rating: ⭐½ out of 5. Great music, brilliant kids, and one of the least qualified teachers in movie history. If this film taught me anything, it’s that confidence can apparently replace a teaching degree.

Of course there are great touches, but it’s rare that it’s engaging. The whole thing is caught in denial of its ridiculousness. The man has no job but has the funds for the instruments. A thousand people at a weekday battle of the bands. Nobody hearing a drum kit outside of the room. Even as a kid the idea of how grounded the photography and style is completely clashed with the story in a way I couldn’t explain but meant I couldn’t get behind it. I’m good with it not making sense, but not if you’re asking for emotional investment. Do it like Scott Pilgrim and support the zaniness with a style. There’s no credibility to the setting but the style insists on capturing this “reality” feel that doesn’t work for me. Remake it animated and do it way weirder with a fully original set of songs in a secondary world and you’re in business.

This had been on my blind spot list for a really long time, most people I know saw it when we were teenagers and it came out but I hated Jack Black at the time and so I wasn't interested. But it's become such a beloved movie that I always meant to rewatch it and hoped that I would also love it. After all, I have seen Jack Black in multiple things now where I really liked him? Anyway, alas that did not happen. Things I DID enjoy included the kids (most of whom weren't amazing actors, the best was definitely the future iCarly, but they were all very cute) and of course Joan Cusack who is a goddess and I love her. Buuuuuuuuuuuuuut... it turns out I still find young Jack Black irritating beyond reason. He feels like one of those guys to me that needs like... a bit of a leash on him. Like call cut more often, don't just keep letting him riff (I feel strongly the same way about Jim Carrey). And even when I would occasionally be like 'okay this is kind of sweet with the kids' he would invariably take it well beyond what I thought was sweet or funny. So kind of a disappointment unfortunately.

“If you wanna rock, you gotta break the rules.” The Rock lesson montage sums up this movie for me. Very childlike understanding of rock music, and I’m sure I would’ve liked this more as a kid, but it doesn’t hit as an adult. I even read that the writer, Mike White, is not a huge fan of classic rock music, and the movie was basically made so Jack Black could do his thing and perform. Of course, even though it wasn’t more than a surface-level, cute comedy, I’ll always appreciate a story about teaching life lessons through unconventional and nontraditional means. The intergenerational thing can be done well, but my adult brain can’t fathom this happening lol. Jack Black singing the Good Times theme song was a pleasant surprise, but I didn’t enjoy this like I thought I would. With ACT III on the horizon, this irritated me a little bit lmao. I’ve seen parts of it over the years and always wanted to see it because I was the age demographic for it when it came out. Still, I can see why people like this. This is one of Jack Black’s most memorable roles for a reason.

We ended up watching School of Rock as it is hard nowadays to find a movie that is enjoyable for the whole family. In reading reviews, I noticed that either folks can't stand the movie or love the film to death.  Anyway it's a middle of the road for me.  A curious entry in Linklater's work. At the end of the movie, my music-loving kid noted that a fully devoted rockaholic would have had a more indie vibe and worshiped an arcane rock band. Would probably dislike "mainstream" groups. True. In that sense, this film is a mainstream film about a misbehaving adult man.  It is sort of a breakout role for Jack Black and it is very much about him more than the kids. (I liked the understated menacing Jack Black in Bernie . Clearly, Richard Linklater found him far more interesting than other other directors). Comedians are fun in this film. Joan Cusack is hilarious in her role as a principal who should honestly be fired. Sarah Silverman plays it straight as a nagging girlfriend. Funnily, she is the bad guy, but is absolutely correct in her assessments and actions. Since I watched it twenty years later, I looked up what the kids are up to. Turns out that drummer kid ( Kevin Clark ) became a musician in real life and tragically passed away in an accident. Life is so short :(

"School of Rock" Director: Richard Linklater Writer: Mike White Cinematography: Rogier Stoffers Editing: Sandra Adair Music: Craig Wedren Starring: Jack Black, Joan Cusack, Mike White, Sarah Silverman, Miranda Cosgrove, Joey Gaydos Jr. Runtime: 109 minutes Release: 2003 A comedy about rock music that understands why music matters "School of Rock" is one of those rare studio comedies that feels almost effortless even though nearly everything about it is carefully constructed. On paper, the premise is ridiculous: a broke, immature guitarist impersonates a substitute teacher at an elite prep school, discovers that his students can play instruments, and secretly turns the class into a rock band so he can enter a competition. In lesser hands, the concept could easily have become nothing more than a vehicle for Jack Black’s enormous personality. Instead, Richard Linklater and screenwriter Mike White turn it into a warm, funny, and surprisingly sincere film about creativity, confidence, education, collaboration, and the importance of discovering something that makes you want to participate in the world. What makes "School of Rock" endure is that it never treats rock music simply as decoration. The guitars, songs, records, and musical references are obviously part of the film’s personality, but music gradually becomes the language through which the children discover abilities and identities that their highly structured school environment has not encouraged. Dewey Finn initially sees the students as tools he can use to return to the stage, but the more time he spends with them, the more his selfish obsession begins to transform into genuine mentorship. He starts noticing their fears, insecurities, strengths, and personalities, and the film becomes as much about Dewey learning how to care about other people as it is about the children learning how to play rock. Direction: Richard Linklater makes chaos feel natural Richard Linklater is an unexpectedly perfect director for this material because his filmmaking has always been interested in character, conversation, time, and people gradually revealing themselves through interaction. Those instincts keep *School of Rock* grounded even when Jack Black is operating at maximum intensity. Linklater does not attempt to compete with Black’s energy through frantic filmmaking. Instead, he creates a stable environment around him and allows the collision between Dewey’s enormous personality and the rigid world of Horace Green to generate the comedy naturally. The classroom feels like a genuine space rather than a stage built around a comedian. The students react individually to Dewey, and Linklater gives them enough screen time to become recognizable people rather than a collection of child actors waiting for Jack Black to deliver another punchline. This becomes essential as the story progresses because the emotional climax depends on our understanding that the band belongs to all of them, not just to Dewey. Linklater’s restraint is especially important because the premise could easily have become exhausting. Dewey is loud, impulsive, and constantly performing, so the direction wisely refuses to make the entire film behave the same way. By keeping the camera relatively grounded and allowing performances to dominate, Linklater makes the chaos feel spontaneous rather than manufactured. The screenplay: selfishness gradually becomes mentorship Mike White’s screenplay is much smarter than its broad comedy premise initially suggests. Dewey is not introduced as an unconventional but secretly brilliant teacher. He is genuinely irresponsible. He lies to obtain the substitute-teaching position, neglects the curriculum, exploits the students for his own ambitions, and initially views the entire class primarily as a way of returning to the Battle of the Bands. That selfishness gives the character somewhere meaningful to develop. Dewey never becomes a conventionally mature adult, nor does the screenplay strip away the qualities that make him ridiculous. Instead, his transformation occurs through attention. He begins listening to the students, discovering what each of them needs, and realizing that helping them become confident matters more than simply using their talents to make himself look good. The screenplay handles this development through small interactions rather than moralizing speeches. Dewey notices that Lawrence worries he is not cool enough to belong in a rock band and immediately reassures him that his musical ability makes him valuable. He recognizes Tomika’s extraordinary voice beneath her insecurity and gives her a space where she can use it without being embarrassed. He understands Summer’s intense need for responsibility and turns that quality into a strength by making her band manager. Even the students who do not play instruments are given meaningful roles in costumes, lighting, security, and technical support. This is where Dewey accidentally becomes a genuinely effective teacher. He has no formal pedagogical knowledge, but he becomes attentive to who his students are rather than simply what they are expected to achieve. Jack Black: a performance built entirely around commitment Jack Black is the obvious center of "School of Rock", and it is almost impossible to imagine the film working with another actor. Dewey Finn could have been unbearable, but Black makes him lovable because he commits completely to every ridiculous impulse the character possesses. There is no ironic distance between Black and Dewey’s love of rock music. When Dewey hears a great riff, discusses a legendary guitarist, or tries to explain the emotional importance of a song, he behaves as though he is discussing something sacred. His physical performance is just as important as his comic timing. Dewey teaches with his entire body, jumping across the classroom, imitating guitar solos, conducting imaginary bands, singing riffs, dancing, pointing, and reacting to music with almost religious intensity. His enthusiasm becomes contagious because Black never suggests that Dewey’s passion is a joke, even when Dewey himself is ridiculous. There is also more vulnerability in the performance than the film is sometimes given credit for. Dewey has failed as a musician, been rejected by his own band, and has almost no stable adult identity outside his dream of becoming a rock star. His arrogance frequently functions as protection against the possibility that he may simply not be as successful as he imagined he would become. Working with the students gives him a new relationship with music. Instead of needing music exclusively as a vehicle for his own recognition, he begins learning how satisfying it can be to help someone else discover their voice. The children: the film’s real secret weapon The child ensemble is one of the main reasons "School of Rock"remains so enjoyable. The students are not written merely as precocious little adults or as interchangeable comedy props. Each has a recognizable personality, function, and insecurity, which allows the class gradually to become a genuine ensemble. Zack is a gifted guitarist whose creativity is restricted by his father’s expectations. Lawrence doubts that his personality fits the image of a rock musician. Tomika has an extraordinary singing voice but is frightened of being judged. Summer is ambitious, controlling, and extremely organized, qualities that could easily make her irritating but instead become invaluable once she is given responsibility. Miranda Cosgrove’s performance as Summer is particularly funny because she approaches the band with the seriousness of a corporate executive managing a major organization. One of the film’s loveliest decisions is that Dewey finds a role for almost everybody. The project is never limited to the children talented enough to stand at the front of the stage. Lighting, costumes, security, management, and technical work all become part of the band's identity. The message is therefore not simply that every child is secretly a musical genius. It is that a creative community becomes stronger when people discover where their abilities fit within something larger than themselves. Rock music is often associated with individual rebellion, but "School of Rock" ultimately turns that rebellion into collaboration. Education: the wrong teacher who understands something important "School of Rock" is not really an argument that formal education is bad, nor does it suggest that Dewey’s deception is acceptable simply because the children enjoy his classes. What the film does criticize is an educational environment that can become so focused on achievement, discipline, and measurable success that it leaves little space for experimentation. Horace Green is prestigious and academically demanding, but many of its students have internalized anxieties about perfection, parental approval, appearance, and failure. Dewey enters the school as perhaps the least qualified person imaginable, yet he introduces something the institution appears to lack: permission to experiment without immediately worrying about whether the result is correct. He allows the children to make noise, fail, try again, and discover talents that have nothing to do with grades. More importantly, he treats their creative interests seriously. He does not condescendingly praise them adults sometimes praise children for doing something cute. When Zack writes music, Dewey treats him like a songwriter. When Tomika sings, he treats her like a vocalist. When Summer manages the band, he treats her like a manager. That respect matters because children can often recognize the difference between an adult who is humoring them and an adult who genuinely believes what they are doing has value. Rock music as a philosophy The film understands rock as more than a musical genre. For Dewey, it represents freedom, authenticity, rebellion, collaboration, and the right to resist identities imposed by other people. His lectures on rock history are funny because he treats them with absurd seriousness, but underneath the comedy lies a sincere belief that art can provide a language for emotions people otherwise struggle to express. This becomes especially important for Zack. He lives under a father who already seems to have determined what kind of future his son should pursue. Writing and performing music gives Zack a means of expressing himself outside that structure. Tomika’s singing allows her to occupy space with confidence rather than apologizing for herself, while Lawrence discovers that musical talent can give him a sense of belonging even if he does not resemble his own idea of what a rock musician should be. The children are therefore not simply learning old songs because the filmmakers enjoy classic rock. They are learning that creativity can become a way of defining yourself rather than accepting every definition other people have already created for you. Cinematography: staying out of the way of performance Rogier Stoffers’ cinematography is deliberately unobtrusive, which is exactly the right choice for the film. The visual style does not attempt to compete with Jack Black’s performance or the energy of the music. Instead, the camera provides enough stability and spatial clarity for the performances to remain the focus. The classroom scenes are particularly effective because the arrangement of the children gradually changes as the band develops. Early in the film, Dewey dominates the room as an outsider imposing his personality on the students. As the children become more confident, the classroom begins to feel increasingly communal, with the ensemble occupying more of the frame as active participants rather than passive listeners. The concert material naturally becomes more dynamic, but even there the film prioritizes readable performance over excessive montage. We can see the children playing together, understand where they are positioned onstage, and experience the performance as something genuinely collective. That clarity helps sell the essential fantasy of the film: these children have actually become a band. Editing: comedy built through rhythm Sandra Adair’s editing is crucial because so much of "School of Rock" depends on rhythm. Jack Black produces an enormous amount of verbal and physical energy, and the editing knows when to remain with him and when the funniest choice is to cut to the children silently processing whatever ridiculous statement he has just made. Their reactions frequently become punchlines in themselves. The editing also handles the musical progression effectively. The band does not immediately sound polished. Rehearsal scenes gradually introduce individual components before allowing them to come together, which gives the final performance a genuine sense of progression. We have watched these children learn how to function as a group, so the concert feels like the culmination of work rather than a magical transformation produced by the screenplay. Adair also balances several tonal modes without making the film feel fragmented. Broad comedy, school satire, musical rehearsal, family conflict, and emotional vulnerability move easily into one another because the pacing never treats them as entirely separate kinds of movies. Joan Cusack: repression slowly cracking open Joan Cusack’s Principal Mullins is one of the film’s best supporting performances because she initially appears to represent everything Dewey rejects. She is formal, anxious, controlled, and deeply concerned with preserving Horace Green’s reputation. Her entire identity seems constructed around behaving exactly as she believes a prestigious school principal should behave. The film gradually reveals that this rigidity is also a performance. Mullins has suppressed parts of herself in order to maintain authority, and the moments when those parts begin slipping through are hilarious because Cusack plays them with incredible precision. Her reactions are never broad enough to destroy the character’s credibility, which contrasts her public and private personalities even funnier. She also reinforces one of the film’s broader ideas: children are not the only people trapped by expectations. Adults can become equally imprisoned by roles they believe they have to perform. Dewey’s chaotic presence disrupts not only the students but also an adult who has forgotten that she once possessed interests beyond professional responsibility. Comedy: why the film remains funny A major reason "School of Rock" has aged so well is that most of its comedy comes from character rather than topical references. Dewey is funny because of the intensity with which he experiences music and his complete inability to recognize normal professional boundaries. Summer is funny because she approaches a school band with the seriousness of an executive managing a multinational company. Mullins is funny because she is desperately trying to prevent her carefully controlled personality from collapsing. The humor also rarely depends on humiliating the children. Dewey may tease them, but when genuine insecurity appears, his attitude changes. The film understands the difference between joking with someone and turning their vulnerability into the joke. That warmth allows the comedy to become affectionate without losing its edge. The movie can recognize that practically everyone in it is ridiculous while still respecting them. Parents, expectations, and identity The parents become increasingly important because they represent another layer of expectations surrounding the children. Zack’s father is the clearest example, having already imagined a particular future for his son and regarding creative interests as distractions from that path. The film does not spend enough time with every parent to develop each family dynamic deeply, but collectively they represent an adult tendency to decide what success should look like before children have had enough life experience to understand what they actually care about. This gives the final concert additional meaning. The children are not only performing for an audience; they are revealing versions of themselves that developed outside direct parental supervision. Their parents suddenly have to confront abilities, interests, and confidence they did not necessarily know existed. The Battle of the Bands therefore becomes a form of self-definition. The Battle of the Bands: succeeding without needing to win One of the smartest choices in Mike White’s screenplay is the decision not to make conventional victory necessary. A lesser version of "School of Rock" would require the children to win the competition because the trophy would function as proof that Dewey’s methods were correct. That would actually weaken the film’s message. The children have already succeeded before the result is announced. They walk onto a stage, perform something they helped create, work together under enormous pressure, and experience the joy of having an audience respond to them. The official competition result therefore becomes secondary to the internal transformation that has already occurred. This reinforces the film’s broader argument about creativity. Art does not become meaningful only when an institution gives it first place. The value can exist in making something, sharing it, and discovering what the process changes inside you. Dewey’s transformation: from wanting attention to learning how to give it Dewey begins the film desperate for an audience. Almost every aspect of his personality is organized around wanting people to watch him play, recognize his talent, and confirm his identity as a serious musician. Even his decision to form the children’s band initially emerges from that same selfish desire. By the ending, he remains loud, theatrical, and unmistakably Dewey, but something important has changed. He has learned how to share the stage. His love of music is no longer exclusively about expressing himself; it has become something he can give to other people. That is the real character arc. Dewey does not mature by abandoning rock and becoming a conventional, responsible adult. He matures by discovering a more generous form of the passion he already possessed. Teaching changes him because it transforms enthusiasm into responsibility. For the first time, his musical knowledge and energy become useful to people other than himself. Linklater’s humanism The film fits surprisingly comfortably within Richard Linklater’s wider body of work because beneath the studio-comedy framework is his familiar fascination with people discovering themselves through conversation, community, and time spent together. Linklater rarely approaches characters with contempt, even when they behave foolishly. That generosity is crucial to "School of Rock". Dewey could easily have been treated simply as a loser, Mullins as nothing more than an uptight authority figure, and the children as recognizable school stereotypes. Instead, each is allowed enough humanity to become more complicated. Linklater’s direction suggests that people can change without needing to become completely different people. Dewey remains Dewey, Summer remains intensely ambitious, and Mullins remains a serious principal. Growth does not require erasing personality; it requires learning how to use that personality differently. Why the film still works The central idea of "School of Rock" has aged remarkably well because children still need opportunities to discover what they care about before adults decide what they should become. The specific rock references may belong largely to previous generations, but the emotional experience is timeless. Every child understands wanting to discover something they are good at. Every teenager understands the frustration of feeling that adults have already planned a future on their behalf. Every artist understands the excitement of realizing that something private can become communal when other people join in. That is the feeling the film captures so effectively. It is not ultimately about creating professional musicians. It is about discovering the thing that makes you excited enough to practice, collaborate, fail, improve, and show up again. Conclusion "School of Rock" remains one of the great feel-good comedies of the early 2000s because it never confuses optimism with emptiness. Beneath Jack Black’s enormous performance and the film’s infectious music is a thoughtful story about education, creativity, confidence, mentorship, and the importance of adults who notice what children might become rather than simply informing them what they should become. Richard Linklater directs with enough restraint to keep the film grounded while allowing Jack Black to operate at full intensity. Mike White’s screenplay gives Dewey a meaningful transformation without removing the immaturity and eccentricity that make him entertaining, while Sandra Adair’s editing balances comedy, music, and emotional development with remarkable ease. The child ensemble gives the film its heart because each student is allowed to become a participant in the story rather than merely an accessory to Dewey’s journey. Most importantly, the greatest thing Dewey gives the students is not musical ability, because many of them already possess talent before he enters the classroom. What he gives them is permission to take that talent seriously. He gives them permission to be loud, to fail, to experiment, to occupy space, and to discover versions of themselves that may not fit comfortably within the expectations surrounding them. The children return that gift by giving Dewey something he has spent much of his adult life searching for without understanding what he actually needed. They give his love of music a purpose beyond his own ego. He finally discovers that standing onstage does not become less meaningful when somebody else receives the applause, and that sharing his passion can be more satisfying than demanding recognition for it. That is why "School of Rock" remains so joyful. It understands that enthusiasm becomes truly meaningful when it becomes generosity, creativity becomes more powerful when it becomes community, and sometimes the teacher who appears completely wrong for the classroom can still teach something valuable because he is the first adult willing to take a child's passion seriously.
